title: Ureter Anatomy
descriptor: Course, Wall, Blood Supply, Peristalsis & Stones
intro: The ureters are a pair of narrow muscular tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder. Each lies behind the peritoneum, running down in front of the psoas muscle and over the pelvic brim before following the wall of the pelvis to the bladder. Urine does not simply drain along them; waves of muscular contraction, called peristalsis, propel it. Where each ureter reaches the bladder it passes obliquely through the wall, an arrangement that helps to stop urine flowing back.

keyFacts.label: Course
keyFacts.value: Retroperitoneal; from the renal pelvis in front of psoas, over the pelvic brim, then along the pelvic side wall to the bladder

keyFacts.label: Length
keyFacts.value: Roughly 25 to 30 cm, following an S-shaped course

keyFacts.label: Relations
keyFacts.value: Right ureter beside the ascending colon, caecum and appendix; left beside the descending and sigmoid colon

keyFacts.label: Wall
keyFacts.value: Transitional epithelium on a fibroelastic lamina propria, a muscular coat and an outer adventitia; no submucosa

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Segmental: aortic, renal, gonadal and common iliac sources above; superior and inferior vesical arteries in the pelvis

keyFacts.label: Urine transport
keyFacts.value: Pushed along by peristaltic waves rather than draining passively

keyFacts.label: Bladder entry
keyFacts.value: Passes obliquely through the bladder wall, forming a one-way physiological sphincter against backflow

sections.heading: Course and relations
sections.body: Each ureter leaves the kidney at the hilum, continuing downwards from the renal pelvis, and its abdominal part is retroperitoneal throughout. It passes in front of the psoas muscle, crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, and then follows the lateral wall of the pelvis before joining the bladder. The course is S-shaped, and the length is roughly 25 to 30 cm. The kidneys and ureters are fully retroperitoneal, whereas the bladder has peritoneum only over its dome. On the right the ureter lies beside the ascending colon, caecum and appendix, and on the left beside the descending and sigmoid colon. Where a uterus is present, the uterine artery crosses in front of the lower part of the ureter, a relationship surgeons sometimes call water under the bridge.

sections.heading: Wall structure
sections.body: The wall of the ureter has three layers: an inner mucosa, a muscular coat and an outer adventitia. The mucosa is lined by stratified transitional epithelium that rests on a relatively thick, fibroelastic lamina propria. There is no submucosa and there are no glands. The muscular coat is made of smooth muscle and drives the peristaltic waves that move urine along. The outer adventitia is made of dense collagen and elastic fibres and holds the smaller blood vessels, lymphatics and nerves of the ureter.

sections.heading: Blood supply, nerves and lymph
sections.body: The blood supply of the ureter is segmental, with different vessels feeding its upper and lower parts. The abdominal part is supplied from the abdominal aorta and from the renal, gonadal and common iliac arteries, while the pelvic part depends on the superior and inferior vesical arteries, which are branches of the internal iliac artery. These vessels join one another in a plexus that runs within the adventitia along the ureter, and the exact arterial pattern varies between individuals. Lymph drains to the internal, external and common iliac nodes; the left ureter also drains towards the left para-aortic nodes, and the right mainly towards the right paracaval and interaortocaval nodes. The ureter receives both sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves.

sections.heading: Peristalsis and the entry into the bladder
sections.body: Urine does not passively drain from the kidney to the bladder; it is propelled by waves of peristalsis. Near the bladder each ureter turns medially and pierces the bladder wall at an angle. This oblique passage works as a one-way, physiological sphincter that lets urine in while blocking backflow. The two ureteric openings form two corners of the trigone, with the opening of the urethra forming the third, and they can be seen at cystoscopy. A recent CT and cadaver study describes the ureterovesical junction as a valve-like structure against reflux and reports that its segment inside the bladder wall is the narrowest part of the upper urinary tract. Children whose ureters lack this oblique course are prone to vesicoureteral reflux and to a higher risk of serious urinary tract infection.

sections.heading: Stones and other conditions
sections.body: Textbooks describe three narrow points in the ureter where a stone is most likely to lodge: the ureteropelvic junction, the point where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels near the pelvic brim, and the ureterovesical junction. The pelvic brim is not a true anatomical constriction, but longer stones may have difficulty passing the sharp angle where the ureter dips into the pelvis. In a study of people attending an emergency department with colic, most stones lay at the ureterovesical junction. A CT-based analysis argues that the three-narrowing concept is incomplete and reports only two common obstruction sites, the upper ureter and the ureterovesical junction. Ultrasound shows stones at the ureteropelvic and ureterovesical junctions well, but stones between the two are extremely difficult to see on ultrasound. Urothelial cells line the ureters, renal pelvis, bladder and urethra, and cancers that begin in them are called urothelial or transitional cell carcinomas.
